## storyScenes/chapter12-mission4-scene3

The Sumuroy marker describes an uprising beginning at Palapag in 1649 and spreading to other places. Spread is a historical claim about a wider reach, not proof that every resident of those places joined. Different local actions and degrees of involvement need their own evidence.

Our fictional source desk compares a place mentioned in an account with a list of named people. A place entry helps locate a reported event; a name entry can support recorded participation. Neither reveals every private motive.

Do not use a regional label as a vote by all households, or turn later administrative boundaries into exact historical areas of control. A movement may affect people who never joined.

To explain a particular town, seek its dated records and compare the actions described. The desk is not a reconstruction of Sumuroys participant register.

Open the three clues, then choose the explanation they support. Use Explain for help or return to this lesson before targeted practice.

## storyScenes/chapter12-mission4-scene4

People in a community could face different resources, responsibilities and pressures. A leader, participant and affected resident did not necessarily have the same options. Historical agency means people could act within conditions, not that everyone had equal power or unlimited freedom.

Compare fictional role cards: one records an organizing action and another records a household affected by events. Identify only what the cards support. Do not assign roles automatically from gender, religion, ancestry or occupation.

Nor should a lack of a famous name make a persons experience unimportant. These cards do not invent a real historical family or ask learners to disclose family income or identity.

To explain an actual case, keep the person, place, period, action and evidence together. Claims about voluntary participation or pressure require evidence rather than a guess from a label.

Open the three clues, then choose the explanation they support. Use Explain for help or return to this lesson before targeted practice.

## storyScenes/chapter12-mission4-scene5

A participation report should identify who is recorded, what action is described and what remains uncertain. A later marker can commemorate a leader without listing all participants. A movement span can extend beyond its founder. Sources about different places and stages should not be merged into one complete community biography.

CulturEd notes that the Dagohoy movement continued after its founder, while the Gabriela marker records a specific leadership continuation in another case. These examples are not the same event or proof of a shared command.

Our fictional portfolio separates leadership evidence, a participation record and an account of affected residents. Match the question to the source, check its date and purpose, and state a limit.

Do not invent a universal national program, private conversations or membership where the evidence is incomplete. Later Mission 5 will examine outcomes and significance.

Open the three clues, then choose the explanation they support. Use Explain for help or return to this lesson before targeted practice.

## storyScenes/chapter12-mission4-scene6

Review five ideas. A leader was not the whole community. Gabriela Silangs continuation keeps her leadership visible and illustrates a movement changing leaders. Spread did not mean every resident joined. Different roles came with different conditions and pressures. Sources have scope and cannot automatically supply every participants story.

## storyScenes/chapter12-mission5-scene1

An aim is what people hope to change. An outcome is what happens. Keep these in separate boxes in your evidence journal. A movement can oppose a policy without removing that policy everywhere. A record of protest tells us that people acted; it does not by itself prove that every demand was achieved.

Use the early revolts from this chapter as case studies. First name the concern, then the action, then a result actually supported by a source. If the result is not supplied, mark it as a question to investigate.

Do not fill the empty box with a victory or defeat you have guessed. People and communities mattered even when their aims were not fully reached. Explaining an outcome carefully is different from giving people a score for winning a battle.

Open the three clues. Choose the explanation supported by the evidence. Use Explain when you need help, then try your decision again.

## storyScenes/chapter12-mission5-scene2

The movement associated with Francisco Dagohoy in Bohol lasted from 1744 to 1829. CulturEd describes communities and local governments linked to the movement. This is evidence of sustained organization. A movement lasting many years can have changing leaders, circumstances and results. Its length is useful evidence, but it is not the same as a list of every aim achieved.

The same account says the movement continued after Dagohoy and that his date of death is uncertain. Do not treat the movement dates as his lifespan or say he personally led every year. Ask a smaller, clearer question: Did organization continue?

That is different from asking whether colonial rule ended throughout the Philippines. Keep the place, period and kind of achievement in your explanation. One word such as successful needs a clear meaning and supporting evidence.

Open the three clues. Choose the explanation supported by the evidence. Use Explain when you need help, then try your decision again.

## storyScenes/chapter12-mission5-scene3

A report about a leader does not tell the whole story of a community. After resistance, families and participants might have different experiences. To investigate effects, look for records about the people, place and time you are describing. Do not invent the fate of an unnamed household from the fate of a leader. An honest answer can identify what is known and what still needs evidence.

Compare two teaching cards: one records a change of leadership and the other asks what happened to local households. These are different questions. A leadership change can be established by a biography, while a household question needs evidence about those households.

A missing account does not mean that people felt nothing or that everyone had the same experience. Studying outcomes includes asking about ordinary people, with respect for the limits of surviving records. These cards are modern learning tools, not historical household records.

Open the three clues. Choose the explanation supported by the evidence. Use Explain when you need help, then try your decision again.

## storyScenes/chapter12-mission5-scene4

The National Museum describes paintings of the Basi Revolt of 1807. The paintings were made in 1821, after the event. They later received recognition as National Cultural Treasure in 2009. Put these on three separate timeline cards: event, representation and later recognition. They answer different historical questions.

A later painting can help us study how an event was represented. It is not a photograph made during the revolt. Museum recognition tells us about later cultural value; it does not tell us that the participants won every demand in 1807.

When you use an image, ask when it was made and what kind of source it is. Our diagram is a modern teaching timeline, not one of the historical paintings.

You can value a work of art while still checking the evidence for an event. Do not mix up the date of an event with the date of its remembrance.

Open the three clues. Choose the explanation supported by the evidence. Use Explain when you need help, then try your decision again.

## storyScenes/chapter12-mission5-scene5

Early resistance helps us investigate concerns about colonial policies, authority, belief and local life. Comparing cases shows differences in place, time, action and participation. A movement can matter to history even when a particular aim was not achieved. Its significance needs an explanation connected to evidence, rather than a label such as winner or loser.

Build a short museum label: name the case, state one supported result, and explain what it helps us understand. Keep later remembrance separate. Do not claim that all early revolts shared one national plan or that a later event was certain to happen.

Similar concerns do not prove that separate movements worked together. Later chapters will examine changing ideas with their own evidence. Your job now is to make a fair explanation of early resistance, including differences and unanswered questions.

This is historical investigation, not a contest about which community was best.

This is evidence of sustained organization. A movement lasting many years can have changing leaders, circumstances and results. Its length is useful evidence, but it is not the same as a list of every aim achieved.

## storyScenes/chapter13-mission1-scene1

The 18th century runs from 1701 to 1800. A year beginning with 17 usually belongs here, but the boundary matters: 1800 is still in the 18th century, while 1801 begins the 19th. Place a date before making a claim about its period. Our timeline is a modern learning tool, not an old calendar.

This mission introduces selected changes rather than every event in one hundred years. Compare trade connections, a temporary occupation and a government monopoly. They concern different parts of life and did not all begin together.

An earlier event does not automatically cause a later one. Keep a question beside each date: what changed, where did it change, and what evidence supports the connection? You will investigate detailed reforms and new ideas in the later missions.

Open the three clues. Select a supported explanation. Use Explain for help and return to these clues before practice.

## storyScenes/chapter13-mission1-scene2

Manila was one end of the Manila-Acapulco galleon route. The Intramuros Administration dates this route from 1571 to 1815. It therefore existed before the 18th century and continued through it. The year 1815 belongs to the next century. A route can continue while other parts of life change.

Trade links show movement between places. They do not tell us that every household was wealthy or that everyone traded directly with Acapulco. A route map answers a question about connections; records about workers and households answer other questions.

Imagine comparing a route card with a local household account. These are teaching examples, not surviving records supplied in this scene. Use each for the question it can support. Do not claim that international connections began only when a later policy was announced.

Open the three clues. Select a supported explanation. Use Explain for help and return to these clues before practice.

## storyScenes/chapter13-mission1-scene3

The Intramuros Administration records a British occupation from 1762 to 1764 during the Seven Years War. This was a temporary political change in Manila. Political questions concern authority: who governed or controlled a place, and when? Locate the event on the same century timeline as the trade route.

Be careful about scale. Evidence about occupation in Manila does not prove that British forces governed every community throughout the islands. A capital city and an entire archipelago are not the same area. Nor does a temporary occupation establish permanent independence.

Ask for the place and period whenever you explain control. You can investigate political change without reenacting a battle. No points are earned for harm; your task is to choose a statement that fits the source and identify what it does not establish.

Open the three clues. Select a supported explanation. Use Explain for help and return to these clues before practice.

## storyScenes/chapter13-mission1-scene4

The government tobacco monopoly was established in 1782 under Governor Jose Basco y Vargas. The National Tobacco Administration describes government efforts to raise revenue, or income for public authorities. This is an example of political decisions shaping economic activity: rules about a crop affected production and selling.

The same historical account describes compulsory planting, quotas and complaints in affected areas. A quota means a required amount. Do not assume every community grew the crop or that all farmers had identical experiences. Government income and household wellbeing are different questions.

Study how a rule could limit choices rather than treating revenue as proof that everyone benefited. Tobacco is discussed only as historical evidence, not as a product to use. You will not grow, buy or try it in this learning activity.

Open the three clues. Select a supported explanation. Use Explain for help and return to these clues before practice.

## storyScenes/chapter13-mission1-scene5

A government can announce a rule before it is put into practice. The NHCP marker for the tobacco monopoly distinguishes a royal decree in 1780 from formal establishment in March 1782. These dates belong to different stages. Do not combine them into one date or assume that a decree immediately changed every local activity.

Use three investigation cards: decision, implementation and experience. A decree helps identify an official decision. An implementation record helps establish when a system started operating. Accounts of affected people help examine its effects. The cards here are modern teaching categories.

A later account also reports abolition in 1882, outside this mission period; it must not be placed in the 18th century. In later missions you will compare reforms more closely.

For now, distinguish what a government intended, what it put into practice and what people experienced.

Open the three clues. Select a supported explanation. Use Explain for help and return to these clues before practice.

## storyScenes/chapter13-mission1-scene6

The 18th century runs from 1701 to 1800. A year beginning with 17 usually belongs here, but the boundary matters: 1800 is still in the 18th century, while 1801 begins the 19th. Place a date before making a claim about its period. Our timeline is a modern learning tool, not an old calendar.

Be careful about scale. Evidence about occupation in Manila does not prove that British forces governed every community throughout the islands. A capital city and an entire archipelago are not the same area. Nor does a temporary occupation establish permanent independence.

Ask for the place and period whenever you explain control. You can investigate political change without reenacting a battle. No points are earned for harm; your task is to choose a statement that fits the source and identify what it does not establish.

Use three investigation cards: decision, implementation and experience. A decree helps identify an official decision. An implementation record helps establish when a system started operating. Accounts of affected people help examine its effects. The cards here are modern teaching categories.

A later account also reports abolition in 1882, outside this mission period; it must not be placed in the 18th century. In later missions you will compare reforms more closely.

For now, distinguish what a government intended, what it put into practice and what people experienced.

Review trade, authority, production and policy stages before the quiz. Missions 2-4 and the chapter challenge are being prepared. Completing one mission does not complete the chapter.

## storyScenes/chapter13-mission2-scene1

A reform changes how something is organized or done. Colonial officials could seek more government income, encourage production or change the organization of trade. These are aims: what a policy was intended to do. The word reform does not prove that a change was fair or helpful to everyone. We still need to investigate its operation and effects.

Use a three-part journal: aim, method and effect. The aim describes the intended change. The method describes how authorities tried to bring it about. The effect concerns what followed for particular people or activities. These parts can differ.

A policy might raise income while placing burdens on producers. An official statement helps establish an aim, but accounts of affected people help investigate experience. The journal is a modern teaching tool, not a surviving colonial report.

Your task is to compare evidence rather than praise every new rule.

Open the three clues. Choose the explanation supported by the evidence. Use Explain if you need help, then return to your decision.

## storyScenes/chapter13-mission2-scene2

Under Jose Basco y Vargas, the Sociedad Economica de los Amigos del Pais was established in 1781. A modern historical study places it within efforts to encourage agriculture and industry. Agriculture concerns growing crops and raising animals; industry includes making and processing goods. Practical knowledge could be used to improve production.

Keep the institution separate from a promise of instant prosperity. Establishing a society does not prove that all farmers received help or that every proposal was carried out. The research also describes periods when the society was inactive, so do not assume continuous success.

Imagine a proposal card beside a record of a completed activity. The proposal shows an intention; the activity record is needed to investigate what was actually done. These example cards are teaching models.

Later achievements must keep their own dates instead of being moved back to the founding year.

Open the three clues. Choose the explanation supported by the evidence. Use Explain if you need help, then return to your decision.

## storyScenes/chapter13-mission2-scene3

The tobacco monopoly offers a concrete example of a government policy affecting production. Established in 1782, it sought government revenue. The National Tobacco Administration historical account describes required planting and quotas, as well as complaints and abuses in affected areas. A quota was a required amount to produce. These details help explain why an income policy could create difficulties for producers.

Distinguish an official goal from a household experience. An official could count income, while a farmer faced a production requirement. Those are different measures of an effect.

Do not assume that every region grew tobacco or that each household experienced the policy in exactly the same way. Ask about the place, time and people in the account. Tobacco is a historical example here, not an invitation to use it.

No activity asks you to grow, buy or try tobacco, and the game gives no points for producing it.

Open the three clues. Choose the explanation supported by the evidence. Use Explain if you need help, then return to your decision.

## storyScenes/chapter13-mission2-scene4

A royal charter dated 10 March 1785 established the Compania de Filipinas, often called the Royal Company of the Philippines. The University Complutense of Madrid preserves a catalogue record for this printed document. This is an example of creating an institution through royal authority. The date and kind of document help us identify an official step in organizing economic activity.

A charter and a record of everyday trade answer different questions. The charter establishes an official authorization; it does not by itself show every shipment, profit or household experience.

We are examining the catalogue description, not pretending to have read every clause of the document. Do not say that this institution instantly replaced every earlier trade connection. In Mission 1 you saw that the Manila-Acapulco route continued until 1815.

New institutions and older practices could exist during overlapping periods. Keep both sets of dates in your journal.

Open the three clues. Choose the explanation supported by the evidence. Use Explain if you need help, then return to your decision.

## storyScenes/chapter13-mission2-scene5

Compare the society, monopoly and company through the same questions. What was established or changed? What method was used? What effects are supported? An organization concerned with economic knowledge, a production monopoly and a royal charter are different kinds of evidence. They should not be treated as three identical solutions or as proof that every community experienced the same change.

For your report, choose one example and write an aim or official step beside a supported effect or an unanswered question. Mark the source for each statement.

If you have only a founding date, do not invent a family story to supply the missing experience. If a source describes a burden, do not erase it because officials had a development goal.

A fair judgement can recognize an intended improvement while examining limits and unequal effects. Later missions will investigate new ideas and grievances; you do not need to claim that one reform made every later event inevitable.

Open the three clues. Choose the explanation supported by the evidence. Use Explain if you need help, then return to your decision.

## storyScenes/chapter13-mission2-scene6

A reform changes how something is organized or done. Colonial officials could seek more government income, encourage production or change the organization of trade. These are aims: what a policy was intended to do. The word reform does not prove that a change was fair or helpful to everyone. We still need to investigate its operation and effects.

For your report, choose one example and write an aim or official step beside a supported effect or an unanswered question. Mark the source for each statement.

## storyScenes/chapter13-mission3-scene1

During the Enlightenment, writers debated reason, learning and the rights of people. They asked questions about government and authority rather than treating every existing rule as beyond discussion. The National Park Service teaching resource describes arguments about freedom of thought, speech and religion. These are examples of ideas to investigate, not a claim that everyone thought alike.

A useful classroom question is: What reason supports this rule, and whom does it affect? Our example is fictional: a reading club must explain why each member may ask a question.

This helps you understand an argument about participation without pretending to be a historical speech. A reasoned argument and an actual change in government are different things. Writings can present an ideal while real societies fall short of it.

Do not assume an idea was entirely new to every society or that one European writer invented all ideas about fairness.

Open the three clues. Choose a supported explanation. Use Explain for help, then review your evidence before practice.

## storyScenes/chapter13-mission3-scene2

In France, the National Assembly adopted the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen in August 1789 during the French Revolution. It stated ideas about liberty and equality before the law. It also addressed representation and the separation of powers. A formal statement allows us to investigate what its authors claimed government should protect.

Equality before the law means that legal treatment should not depend simply on a privileged social position. Separation of powers means dividing government responsibilities rather than putting every task in one pair of hands.

These are simplified explanations of the ideas, not a translation of every article. Keep the place and date with the document. A declaration adopted in France was not automatically a law in the Philippines.

Nor does its adoption prove that every person gained equal treatment in daily life. Ask how a principle was applied and who could actually take part.

Open the three clues. Choose a supported explanation. Use Explain for help, then review your evidence before practice.

## storyScenes/chapter13-mission3-scene3

The Cadiz Constitution was promulgated in Spain in 1812. This date belongs to the 19th century, after the 18th-century changes in Mission 1. The Spanish Senate preserves its text. It divided responsibilities for making laws, carrying them out and deciding legal cases among different institutions. This helps us investigate an alternative to placing all government tasks under unlimited personal authority.

The text also listed the Philippine islands in its description of Spanish territory. This shows a connection between a Spanish constitutional document and the colonial setting of the Philippines.

It does not establish effective control in every community or prove that every resident had the same political rights. The constitution contained restrictions as well as principles. Treat it as a historical document, not the current Philippine Constitution.

Ask separately what a text states, when it operated and what happened locally. One document cannot answer every question about everyday experience.

Open the three clues. Choose a supported explanation. Use Explain for help, then review your evidence before practice.

## storyScenes/chapter13-mission3-scene4

The NCCA account of Philippine literature dates the newspaper Del Superior Gobierno to 1811. Newspapers are one way information can be printed and shared. Printing, circulation, reading and agreement are separate steps. A publication date establishes a printed outlet; it does not identify every reader or tell us that each reader accepted an idea.

The same NCCA account describes colonial regulation of literary production and circulation. Restrictions on materials could affect access to ideas. We should not assume that all writing moved freely.

A person might receive a text, hear a discussion about it or have no access to it. Those are possibilities to investigate, not invented biographies of named students or historical residents.

We do not have the contents of a specific 1811 issue in this scene, so do not claim that it printed a particular rights text. Check an actual issue before making a claim about its contents.

Open the three clues. Choose a supported explanation. Use Explain for help, then review your evidence before practice.

## storyScenes/chapter13-mission3-scene5

Build an idea trail with four cards: a statement is written, a copy travels, someone receives it, and a response is recorded. These are modern teaching cards, not four surviving records supplied by this scene. They show the evidence you would seek before claiming that an international idea influenced a particular person or group. A possible route is not yet proof of a specific influence.

For a fictional example, a club receives a booklet and later writes minutes discussing one of its proposals. The delivery note supports receipt. The minutes support a response. Neither proves that every member agreed or that the booklet alone caused every later decision.

Historical investigations need similar care with real records. Keep the dates, language and audience in view. People can adapt, question or reject an idea. New ideas interacted with local concerns; they did not erase the histories and choices of Philippine communities.

Mission 4 will examine local grievances and growing political awareness.

Open the three clues. Choose a supported explanation. Use Explain for help, then review your evidence before practice.

## storyScenes/chapter13-mission3-scene6

During the Enlightenment, writers debated reason, learning and the rights of people. They asked questions about government and authority rather than treating every existing rule as beyond discussion. The National Park Service teaching resource describes arguments about freedom of thought, speech and religion. These are examples of ideas to investigate, not a claim that everyone thought alike.

## storyScenes/chapter13-mission4-scene1

A local grievance concerns a problem experienced or reported in a particular place. To investigate it, identify who raised the concern, which rule or action it involved, and what change was requested. A general label such as unfairness is a starting point, not a complete explanation. Ask what evidence gives the complaint its specific meaning.

Use this fictional classroom example: a reading club says that one rule keeps some members from borrowing books. The club asks who made the rule and how it might be changed. This connects a practical problem with questions about authority and participation.

It is a teaching example, not a historical petition. Historical grievances need their own records. A complaint may challenge one rule without rejecting every institution.

Political awareness in this mission means thinking about rules, authority and participation; it is not a claim that everyone already supported one national program.

Open the three clues. Choose a supported explanation. Use Explain for help, then review this lesson before practice.

## storyScenes/chapter13-mission4-scene2

Revisit Bacolor, Pampanga, as an earlier comparison. In 1698, Chinese mestizo chiefs petitioned the colonial government for relief from tribute-collection duties. The UP Diliman research summary connects their request with financial pressure from a land-regularization policy. In simple terms, that policy required payment to make landholding legally recognized. Keep the particular request and the people named by the source together.

The year 1698 is in the 17th century. This flashback shows that people could question burdens before the later international documents in Mission 3. It does not establish that they used those later texts or held every later political idea.

A formal request was a way to address an authority; it was not the same action as an armed uprising. A petition also does not prove that its demands were granted.

Do not assign a common motive to everyone from ancestry or a category label. Use the reported action and concern as your evidence.

Open the three clues. Choose a supported explanation. Use Explain for help, then review this lesson before practice.

## storyScenes/chapter13-mission4-scene3

The government tobacco monopoly, established in 1782, connects the reform questions in Mission 2 with local burdens. The National Tobacco Administration account describes compulsory planting, production quotas and complaints in affected areas.

A quota could place a demand on producers even when officials described a policy as a way to raise government income. This is a connection between a rule and a reported difficulty, not proof that everyone had the same experience.

Ask a precise question: What did the policy require, and whose account describes its effects? A government income record and a producers account can concern the same system while answering different questions. Compare them rather than treating income as every households wellbeing.

Do not assume that every region grew the crop or every complaint had the same outcome. Tobacco appears only as historical evidence. This activity does not ask you to grow, buy or use it.

Your task is to explain the relationship between policy and a supported concern.

Open the three clues. Choose a supported explanation. Use Explain for help, then review this lesson before practice.

## storyScenes/chapter13-mission4-scene4

The Basi Revolt in Ilocos in 1807 opposed a government monopoly over basi, a sugarcane wine. The CCP account connects the policy with official control over makers and selling prices. A local product could therefore become part of a dispute about economic choices and colonial authority. Identify the policy connection rather than reducing the concern to a dislike of one official or guessing every persons private motive.

This case also helps distinguish forms of response. A petition is a formal request; the Basi case was an uprising. Similar concerns about burdens do not make the two actions identical or show that their participants coordinated a shared program.

Keep the cases separate before comparing them. Basi is discussed as a historical product, not an invitation to make or drink alcohol. We do not reenact violence or award points for harm.

Your investigation asks which evidence links a particular concern with a particular action, and what still needs more evidence.

Open the three clues. Choose a supported explanation. Use Explain for help, then review this lesson before practice.

## storyScenes/chapter13-mission4-scene5

A recorded request can show people addressing authority about a concern. A reported uprising can show opposition to a policy. These are ways to investigate political awareness through actions and arguments. They do not reveal every private belief. To explain growing awareness over time, compare several dated records and ask what changed in the concerns expressed, the audiences addressed or the forms of participation.

One source cannot prove that everyone became aware at the same moment. Shared grievances do not automatically mean a shared national identity or a coordinated national plan.

International writings could offer ideas to discuss, but claims about influence need evidence of receipt and response, as you learned in Mission 3. Local experiences also matter. Build a report with one supported connection and one honest limit.

For example, distinguish a request for relief from a demand for complete independence. The next chapter will examine national consciousness more closely using its own evidence.

## storyScenes/chapter14-mission1-scene1

A contribution is an action or effort we can identify in a historical account. It might concern organizing a community, continuing leadership or expressing a concern. An outcome is what followed. Keep them separate: a contribution can be studied even when a particular aim was not achieved. A battle result alone does not tell the whole history of a movement.

In this chapter you will connect earlier evidence with questions about a wider sense of belonging. Do not begin by assuming that all early movements shared one national plan. First ask what people actually did in a named place and period.

Then explain what that action helps us understand. A learning journal can contain three boxes: recorded contribution, supported outcome and later remembrance. These boxes are modern teaching tools.

They help you appreciate effort without inventing a victory, a speech or a motive that the source does not supply.

Open the three clues. Choose a supported explanation. Use Explain for help, then revisit the evidence before practice.

## storyScenes/chapter14-mission1-scene2

The movement associated with Francisco Dagohoy in Bohol is dated 1744-1829. CulturEd describes communities and local government linked with it. These details let us investigate organization, not just a single encounter. A movement can involve keeping people and activities together through changing circumstances.

The same account says the movement continued beyond its founder, whose death date is uncertain. The movement dates are not his lifespan. Do not say that he personally led every year or that every resident had the same role.

A useful contribution statement is specific: the account records community organization and continuation. That is different from claiming permanent independence throughout the Philippines. Ask what kind of achievement your evidence supports and which area it concerns.

This lesson values sustained organization without turning duration into proof that every aim succeeded.

Open the three clues. Choose a supported explanation. Use Explain for help, then revisit the evidence before practice.

## storyScenes/chapter14-mission1-scene3

The NHCP registry records that Gabriela Silang continued the Ilocos uprising after Diego Silang. This is a specific example of leadership continuing through a change. It helps us see a contribution that would be missed if a report stopped with only one leader. Keep the named action and its setting together rather than turning a biography into a list of every participant.

The registry describes a marker installed in 1963 about an earlier life and uprising. A later marker can preserve a public account; it is not a transcript of every meeting.

We use the supported continuation claim without inventing dialogue or the thoughts of unnamed residents. Nor does one example mean that all women had the same role or opportunity. Recognizing a named contribution can open further questions about people whose actions need other records.

Later missions will examine participation more closely; you do not need to assign roles from gender, religion or ancestry.

Open the three clues. Choose a supported explanation. Use Explain for help, then revisit the evidence before practice.

## storyScenes/chapter14-mission1-scene4

The National Museum describes paintings of the Basi Revolt of 1807 that were made in 1821. The series received National Cultural Treasure recognition in 2009. These dates show different stages: an event, a later representation and later recognition. Studying remembrance helps us ask how an event has been kept in public memory.

Later recognition is not proof that the participants achieved every demand in the revolt. A painting is also not a photograph taken during the event. Ask when a representation was made, what kind of source it is and what question it can answer.

Our diagram is a modern timeline, not one of the historical paintings. You can value a preserved work while checking its limits as evidence. Remembering resistance and establishing its immediate outcome are different tasks.

Keep both in your journal so that appreciation does not replace careful historical explanation.

Open the three clues. Choose a supported explanation. Use Explain for help, then revisit the evidence before practice.

## storyScenes/chapter14-mission1-scene5

Across these cases, you can investigate organization, changing leadership and remembrance. They offer different kinds of evidence about early resistance. A fair historical lesson names a case, identifies an action or source and explains what it helps us understand. It does not reduce people to winners and losers or rank communities as better than others.

For a fictional classroom example, a history club compares two dated reports and notices that similar concerns led to different responses. Its useful lesson is to examine local conditions rather than assume one response fits every place.

This does not prove that the historical groups coordinated a national program. Later national consciousness needs its own evidence of wider belonging and shared political aims. Early resistance belongs in that longer investigation, but the later outcome was not guaranteed.

Your next missions will compare regions, participation, unity and changing identity through more specific questions.

Open the three clues. Choose a supported explanation. Use Explain for help, then revisit the evidence before practice.

## storyScenes/chapter14-mission2-scene1

A historical place name helps locate an action, but it does not identify every person who took part. A town could include leaders, participants, residents affected by events and people whose actions are not recorded. These groups can overlap. Being present in a place is not the same as joining a movement.

Use a modern evidence desk with three fictional cards: a place label, a named action and an account of an affected household. The place label tells you where to investigate. The named action helps identify participation. The household account would help examine an experience.

These are teaching categories, not authentic registers for the cases in this mission. To describe a community fairly, say which people and actions your source actually records. Do not decide a persons role or motive from a modern regional label, religion or ancestry.

An unnamed person is not automatically a nonparticipant either.

Open the three clues. Choose a supported explanation. Use Explain for help, then return to the evidence before practice.

## storyScenes/chapter14-mission2-scene2

CulturEd places Tamblots uprising in Bohol in 1621. It also describes the movement associated with Dagohoy in Bohol from 1744 to 1829. One place can therefore contain different movements at different times. Put separate case cards on your timeline rather than merging every Bohol action into one continuous event.

The earlier case is connected in its account with religious practice; the later account describes a burial dispute and local organization. These short summaries do not supply every participants beliefs.

Similar themes do not prove that the same people joined both movements or that they followed one unchanged plan. The beginnings are more than a century apart.

Ask the same questions of each case: when, where, who is recorded and what action or concern is described? Respect peoples beliefs while investigating particular actions. This activity asks for evidence comparison, not religious practice or a judgement about which belief is better.

Open the three clues. Choose a supported explanation. Use Explain for help, then return to the evidence before practice.

## storyScenes/chapter14-mission2-scene3

The NHCP marker for Agustin Sumuroy connects the Palapag uprising of 1 June 1649 with forced labor and abuses. It also describes spread beyond the starting place, naming areas in the Visayas, Mindanao and Luzon. This lets us investigate a movement with a wider reported reach rather than treating every case as limited to one town.

Keep the wording of the source in view. Reported spread is not a census of every participant or proof that all communities acted together in the same way.

A marker written later summarizes a history; it does not supply every local meeting or account of coordination. To investigate a named area more closely, seek records about the actions and people there.

Our teaching card lists broad island groups rather than pretending to reconstruct exact routes of travel or command. A line between places on a diagram would not by itself prove who carried a message or how every action was organized.

Open the three clues. Choose a supported explanation. Use Explain for help, then return to the evidence before practice.

## storyScenes/chapter14-mission2-scene4

The NHCP registry records that Gabriela Silang continued the Ilocos uprising after Diego Silang. This identifies a contribution in a particular regional setting. It helps a comparison include leadership changes instead of treating a region as one person or an unchanged group. A regional account can contain different people and stages.

Use the contribution as evidence of the named action. Do not turn it into a complete register of Ilocos residents or assume that everyone supported the same aims. A leader and a whole community are not interchangeable.

The later marker also cannot tell us every unnamed persons role. When comparing this case with Bohol or Palapag, identify what each source actually supplies: a leadership continuation, a movement period or a statement of spread. These are different clues.

Additional records would be needed to describe every contributor or establish coordination between separate cases. Regional variety belongs in the explanation rather than being erased.

Open the three clues. Choose a supported explanation. Use Explain for help, then return to the evidence before practice.

## storyScenes/chapter14-mission2-scene5

Build a portfolio with columns for case, place, period, recorded action and limits. Place Tamblot and the Dagohoy movement on separate Bohol rows. Add the reported spread from the Sumuroy marker and the named leadership continuation in Ilocos. These entries let you recognize different regional experiences without pretending that the sources provide the same detail for each.

A useful portfolio can reveal questions, not only answers. Which account names participants? Which describes a wider reach? Which leaves local coordination unclear? A common concern is worth comparing, but it does not automatically establish one national organization.

Do not rank regions by bravery, participation totals you do not have or battles won. Missing detail in a short source does not make a community less important. The next mission will examine women and Indigenous peoples more closely.

## storyScenes/chapter14-mission3-scene1

The NHCP registry records that Gabriela Silang continued the Ilocos uprising after Diego Silang. This is a specific contribution by a woman in a named movement. A history that stops with Diego would miss that continuation. Begin with the recorded action rather than guessing what someone could do from gender alone.

The source is a later historical marker, not a complete account of every meeting or participant. Recognizing Gabriela does not prove that all women had the same role, opportunity or experience.

Nor does an unnamed woman in a short account automatically mean that women did nothing. Ask which action is recorded and what further evidence would help identify other contributions. You do not need to invent a speech to value a contribution.

This lesson examines leadership respectfully; it does not ask classmates to disclose identity or act out a battle.

## storyScenes/chapter14-mission3-scene2

A UCLA summary of research by Stephen Acabado and Marlon Martin describes Ifugao resistance to Spanish conquest alongside strategies that strengthened local organization. This is a named Indigenous case in the northern Philippines. It challenges an account that treats communities only as people acted upon by outsiders, without decisions of their own.

Agency does not mean unlimited freedom or that every choice was made by everyone equally. Ask what decisions the research supports and how conditions affected them. Do not turn one Ifugao case into the identical history of all Indigenous peoples.

Communities have different histories, institutions and relationships. The summary draws on archaeological investigation and collaboration; it is not a transcript of every persons thoughts. Our diagram is a modern evidence guide, not a reconstruction of a universal Indigenous council.

Keep claims tied to the particular community and evidence.

Open the three clues. Choose a supported explanation. Use Explain for help, then return to this evidence before practice.

## storyScenes/chapter14-mission3-scene3

The Ifugao research summary describes people using colonial economic opportunities to strengthen their organization while resisting Spanish conquest. This lets us examine contact and resistance together. Having an exchange or a connection does not by itself prove that a community gave up all decisions. Isolation and total submission are not the only possibilities to investigate.

Ask separate questions: What connection is recorded? Who made a decision? What evidence shows authority being carried out? A trade connection alone cannot answer all three. The lesson concerns a historical case, not a present-day legal ruling about territory.

Nor does autonomy imply that every resident had equal influence or that a community never changed. Avoid treating Indigenous people as frozen in the past.

Investigate changing strategies and conditions through evidence, without inventing a particular bargain, council vote or shared motive that the summary does not provide.

Open the three clues. Choose a supported explanation. Use Explain for help, then return to this evidence before practice.

## storyScenes/chapter14-mission3-scene4

CulturEd identifies Tamblot as a babaylan who led an uprising in Bohol in 1621. The account connects the case with earlier religious practices. It supplies an example of cultural leadership in a particular place and period. A cultural role can matter to an account of resistance, alongside other forms of leadership and organization.

Do not use the role label to assign the same gender, beliefs or actions to every person called a babaylan. This lesson does not classify Tamblot as a woman or turn the case into every Indigenous communitys story.

The entry acknowledges limited information about his life. A gap is a reason to investigate, not permission to invent dialogue or motives. Studying a religious practice does not require following it or judging a classmates faith.

Our cards describe evidence; they are not instructions for rituals or costumes. Later sources and community knowledge may help answer different questions.

Open the three clues. Choose a supported explanation. Use Explain for help, then return to this evidence before practice.

## storyScenes/chapter14-mission3-scene5

The UCLA research summary emphasizes collaboration with Ifugao communities in studying history and heritage. This matters because a history written only through outside descriptions can miss community knowledge and questions. Archaeological evidence and community participation can help examine earlier interpretations rather than simply repeat them.

For a fictional classroom model, a history team compares a written description, material evidence and a community explanation. Each has a source, context and limits. The model is not an authentic interview or permission to collect sensitive family information.

Different evidence should be examined carefully, not ranked by assuming one identity is always right or wrong. A disagreement calls for respectful questions and further investigation. Your journal should identify whose action is supported, whose perspective is included and what remains unknown.

A fuller account recognizes contributions without assigning everyone the same experience.

## storyScenes/chapter14-mission3-scene6

The NHCP registry records that Gabriela Silang continued the Ilocos uprising after Diego Silang. This is a specific contribution by a woman in a named movement. A history that stops with Diego would miss that continuation. Begin with the recorded action rather than guessing what someone could do from gender alone.

For a fictional classroom model, a history team compares a written description, material evidence and a community explanation. Each has a source, context and limits. The model is not an authentic interview or permission to collect sensitive family information.

Different evidence should be examined carefully, not ranked by assuming one identity is always right or wrong. A disagreement calls for respectful questions and further investigation. Your journal should identify whose action is supported, whose perspective is included and what remains unknown.

A fuller account recognizes contributions without assigning everyone the same experience.

Review Gabrielas recorded action, the Ifugao research and the particular Tamblot case. Keep community, role, source and limits together. Missions 4-5 and the chapter challenge are being prepared. Completing this mission alone does not complete the chapter.

## storyScenes/chapter14-mission4-scene1

People can work together on one concern while having different experiences, beliefs or reasons. Unity does not require everyone to be identical. To investigate it in history, ask what people are recorded as doing together and which aim or action they shared. A modern regional label or a similar complaint alone is not enough to establish a partnership.

Use a fictional classroom model: two reading groups jointly ask for longer library hours. They share that request but prefer different books and have different schedules. Their joint letter is evidence of cooperation on one aim, not proof of agreement about everything.

This is a teaching model, not an authentic colonial petition. In historical cases, identify the particular people, period and action supported by the source. Do not turn one shared request into a complete national program or assume that different backgrounds made cooperation impossible.

Open the three clues. Choose a supported explanation. Use Explain for help, then review the evidence before practice.

## storyScenes/chapter14-mission4-scene2

The NHCP marker for Sumuroy describes the Palapag uprising of 1649 and reported spread into other areas. This supports a question about wider reach. It does not supply every local meeting or plan. A movement spreading and people coordinating particular actions are related questions, but they require different kinds of detail.

Imagine a modern evidence desk with a summary of places and a separate record of a joint plan. The first helps examine reach; the second would help examine coordination. These are teaching categories, not two original records supplied here.

Do not draw an exact command route from a short summary or assume every resident joined. Equally, missing detail in the summary is not proof that no coordination ever occurred. State what the source supports, then mark what needs closer local evidence.

This lets you study connections without making every action identical.

Open the three clues. Choose a supported explanation. Use Explain for help, then review the evidence before practice.

## storyScenes/chapter14-mission4-scene3

The UP Diliman research summary about 17th-century Pampanga describes Chinese mestizos being recognized by local elites as legitimate members of the pueblos, despite legal distinctions. In this setting, a pueblo was a town community. The account connects recognition with family ties and social integration. This helps investigate local belonging instead of treating an official category as a complete description of community relationships.

Keep the scope clear. The summary concerns a particular place, period and social setting; recognition by some local elites is not every residents recorded opinion.

It is not proof that everyone had equal power or that modern national identity already existed in the same form. People can have connections to family, town and wider groups without every connection being identical.

We study the historical categories as terms in a source, not labels to assign to classmates. Do not ask anyone to disclose ancestry or infer a persons loyalty from a category.

Open the three clues. Choose a supported explanation. Use Explain for help, then review the evidence before practice.

## storyScenes/chapter14-mission4-scene4

Differences in aims, resources, risks or opportunities can affect whether people work together. These are questions to investigate in a particular case, not automatic explanations for every movement. A disagreement does not by itself prove that one community was less brave or that every person who did not join was disloyal.

In a fictional classroom model, two groups want better library access but disagree about meeting times because their schedules differ. A record of their discussion could help explain the disagreement. Their background labels alone could not. This model does not describe a historical council.

For real cases, seek evidence of the particular conditions and recorded choices. The Ifugao research from Mission 3 reminds us to examine community decisions within circumstances rather than assume one response for everyone.

Do not invent an internal dispute or treat the model as a single explanation for the outcomes of all early revolts.

Open the three clues. Choose a supported explanation. Use Explain for help, then review the evidence before practice.

## storyScenes/chapter14-mission4-scene5

To investigate a wider shared identity, compare dated records about how people described their group, aims and connections. A source naming one town answers a different question from a document expressing wider political belonging. A shared grievance, a joint action and a collective identity are not interchangeable forms of evidence.

Build a journal with columns for date, group named, action or words recorded and limits. A common concern can make comparison useful without proving coordination. A joint action can show cooperation without revealing every members identity.

An expression of wider belonging still needs its own place and period. Do not arrange the cards as if one local complaint made every later development inevitable. The next mission will examine early developments toward Filipino national consciousness more closely.

For now, identify the scale of each claim and the evidence that would support it, while preserving different community histories.

Open the three clues. Choose a supported explanation. Use Explain for help, then review the evidence before practice.

## storyScenes/chapter14-mission4-scene6

People can work together on one concern while having different experiences, beliefs or reasons. Unity does not require everyone to be identical. To investigate it in history, ask what people are recorded as doing together and which aim or action they shared. A modern regional label or a similar complaint alone is not enough to establish a partnership.

Build a journal with columns for date, group named, action or words recorded and limits. A common concern can make comparison useful without proving coordination. A joint action can show cooperation without revealing every members identity.

## storyScenes/chapter14-mission5-scene1

National consciousness concerns a sense of belonging beyond one household or town and thinking about a wider peoples future. In this lesson it is a concept to investigate through words, actions and connections. It does not mean that everyone has identical experiences, agrees on every policy or uses the same name in every period.

Recall the difference between a shared complaint, cooperation and identity. A joint request can show work on one aim without proving a complete national program.

To examine wider belonging, seek evidence that addresses a wider group or future, then keep the author, audience and date with it. A modern chapter title cannot supply the beliefs of every historical resident.

Our teaching cards are guides to questions, not authentic statements by unnamed people. This mission follows selected developments and later examples; it does not name a single day on which everyone became nationally aware.

Open the three clues. Choose a supported explanation. Use Explain for help, then review the evidence before practice.

## storyScenes/chapter14-mission5-scene2

Earlier petitions and uprisings show people addressing authority and resisting particular burdens. They help us investigate a longer history of public concerns. For example, the 1698 Bacolor petition studied earlier requested relief from tribute-collection duties. The UP Diliman summary identifies a particular group, place and request. It does not turn that request into every later political aim.

Keep both a connection and a limit in your journal. The connection is that earlier people could question burdens and address authority. The limit is that later national consciousness needs evidence of wider belonging and aims in its own period.

Do not put later words into an earlier petition or assume that one complaint caused every later development. Compare records rather than making a straight, guaranteed path. Local histories matter even when they differ from a later national story.

A supported explanation can recognize these foundations while leaving room for different experiences and changing choices.

Open the three clues. Choose a supported explanation. Use Explain for help, then review the evidence before practice.

## storyScenes/chapter14-mission5-scene3

Gomburza refers to Mariano Gomes, Jose Burgos and Jacinto Zamora. The National Parks Development Committee account records their execution by colonial authorities in 1872 after alleged involvement in the Cavite mutiny. Alleged involvement is an accusation, not proof that they organized the mutiny. This lesson does not show or describe the method of their deaths.

The same account records that Rizal dedicated El Filibusterismo to them. This provides a specific connection between an earlier event and later remembrance in writing. It is stronger than simply guessing how every person reacted.

A dedication shows an authors act of honoring; it is not a survey of every reader or proof that the event alone caused a later national movement. Keep event, remembrance and interpretation separate.

You can study why an event mattered without reenacting harm, assuming guilt or requiring anyone to share a religious belief. Seek the particular recorded connection your explanation uses.

Open the three clues. Choose a supported explanation. Use Explain for help, then review the evidence before practice.

## storyScenes/chapter14-mission5-scene4

Rizals Filipinas dentro de cien anos, often known in English as The Philippines a Century Hence, discussed the future of the Philippines. Its publication record places the series in La Solidaridad from September 1889 to January 1890. This is a later 19th-century example of writing about a wider political future rather than only one town request.

The source is an argument by an author, not a prediction we should treat as a guaranteed outcome. Distinguish its original publication period from the later reprint used to preserve the text.

Publication gives evidence that a position was expressed; records of circulation and responses are needed to investigate who encountered it and how they reacted. We use the title, period and broad subject, not every judgement or stereotype in the historical work.

A simplified teaching description is not a quotation from Rizal. Different people could consider, adapt or question a public argument. Do not replace community histories with one authors complete view.

Open the three clues. Choose a supported explanation. Use Explain for help, then review the evidence before practice.

## storyScenes/chapter14-mission5-scene5

Bring the records together without making them identical. An earlier local request, the remembrance of Gomburza and writing about a wider future answer different questions. A timeline orders dates; your explanation must also identify the connection supported by each source. Date order alone does not prove that one event caused the next.

Use four columns: period, source, public concern and limit. The earlier petition concerns particular duties. A dedication records a later act of honoring. A published essay expresses an argument about the Philippines future.

These selected examples help investigate changing scales of concern; they do not show every persons beliefs or make one event the only origin of national consciousness. Community differences and Indigenous histories remain part of the investigation.

Your final challenge will ask you to connect the chapter evidence, recognize contributions and judge the scope of a claim. No community needs to be ranked by bravery or treated as less important because a short source gives fewer details.

Open the three clues. Choose a supported explanation. Use Explain for help, then review the evidence before practice.

## storyScenes/chapter14-mission5-scene6

National consciousness concerns a sense of belonging beyond one household or town and thinking about a wider peoples future. In this lesson it is a concept to investigate through words, actions and connections. It does not mean that everyone has identical experiences, agrees on every policy or uses the same name in every period.

Use four columns: period, source, public concern and limit. The earlier petition concerns particular duties. A dedication records a later act of honoring. A published essay expresses an argument about the Philippines future.

These selected examples help investigate changing scales of concern; they do not show every persons beliefs or make one event the only origin of national consciousness. Community differences and Indigenous histories remain part of the investigation.

Your final challenge will ask you to connect the chapter evidence, recognize contributions and judge the scope of a claim. No community needs to be ranked by bravery or treated as less important because a short source gives fewer details.

## storyScenes/chapter8-mission1-scene6

Explain missionary activity using evidence and respect. Identify the aim of spreading Catholic Christianity without turning that aim into proof of everyone's belief. Separate the 1521 events from the later 1565 arrival example.

Connect a teaching material with an effort to communicate, then distinguish production from reading and reception. Include colonial power and local interests rather than assuming teachings moved without context. A ceremony or writer's account does not reveal every person's thoughts.

Use this fictional report frame in your own words: At [place and period], evidence shows [event or material]. It supports [specific claim] about missionary work or local response. It does not establish [unsupported conclusion]. This is a classroom guide, not an original speech.

## storyScenes/chapter8-mission2-scene6

Explain royal patronage as a relationship rather than a claim that all roles and beliefs became identical. Identify support for religious work, recognized influence in institutional matters and the distinct responsibilities of participants.

Trace the action before judging the outcome. An allocation is not actual delivery; a proposed candidate is not every later approval; a disputed claim is not a final accepted decision. Look for evidence of later actions and effects on people.

Use this fictional report frame in your own words: The record shows [support, role or claim]. It concerns [institution, place and period]. To establish [later outcome or local response], we need [further evidence]. This is a classroom guide, not an original quotation or religious instruction.

## storyScenes/chapter8-mission3-scene6

Explain change by asking what the evidence records and what it leaves uncertain. Separate beliefs from practices and institutions. Keep the beginning of a parish distinct from the age of every visible building feature. Include artisans and local participants in accounts of religious art.

Look for continuity as well as change without inventing identical beliefs for all people. A modern heritage display can be valuable without proving that all of its details existed unchanged during colonial rule. Compare dates and purposes before connecting sources.

Use this fictional report frame in your own words: At [place and time], evidence shows [object, action or institution]. Compared with [other dated evidence], this suggests [supported change or continuity]. It does not establish [unsupported claim]. The frame is not an original quotation.

## storyScenes/chapter8-mission4-scene5

A strong explanation connects a response with evidence and a limit. Try three steps: name the action, give a clue that supports it, and say what the clue does not tell you. Different sources can answer different questions. A dated account may describe an event; an object may help explain work or use. Neither automatically supplies every persons reasons.

In this fictional investigation, one card records work on a new commission and another describes opposition to a demand. You can explain two different actions. You cannot combine them into a claim that all residents agreed, or that every person resisted.

Ask whether the source identifies the same people, place and time. If it does not, keep the cases separate. Saying we need more evidence is a useful finding, not a failure.

Open all three evidence clues, then choose the explanation they support. You may review the clues or use Explain before answering. We assess the explanation, never your own religion or family identity.

## storyScenes/chapter8-mission4-scene6

You have investigated different responses to colonial change. Review five ideas: people could respond differently; change and continuity could go together; Tamblots case belongs to a named place and period; living heritage needs dated evidence; and explanations need support and limits.

Imagine you are preparing a report for another Grade 5 learner. Choose one case and describe the action. Add a supporting clue, then say what you still cannot know. Do not invent private thoughts or treat one community as all communities. You do not need to disclose a belief or act out a conflict.
