## storyScenes/chapter9-mission1-scene1

Tribute was a required payment under Spanish colonial authority. It was not simply a freely chosen present. Collecting it brought resources into the colonial system. To understand a demand, ask who required payment, who was expected to pay, and what rule applied in that place and period. A label such as tax does not tell us whether a collection was fair.

Imagine two fictional cards. One describes a family choosing a gift; the other records a payment demanded by an authority. The second describes an obligation: something people were required to do. Do not call it voluntary just because a record says it was paid.

A payment record also does not show that every resident agreed with the demand. We study this system to understand people and power, not to reward collecting from classmates.

Open the three clues. Then choose the explanation they support. Use Explain if you want help, and return to the lesson before practice when a topic needs review.

## storyScenes/chapter9-mission1-scene2

Payments did not always consist only of coins. Early colonial accounts describe goods such as rice, cotton, cloth and wax being collected as tribute in particular places. The kind of payment depended on the rule and setting. An example of cloth tribute does not mean that every household everywhere paid the same cloth or amount.

A study in The Philippine Review of Economics discusses woven goods in early tribute and trade. This helps keep the work of makers visible: cloth had to be produced before it could be collected.

Our pictured bundle is a modern teaching symbol, not an original tribute item or a measurement guide. When you read a record, look for its place, date, item and unit. Do not change an example into a universal payment schedule.

Open the three clues. Then choose the explanation they support. Use Explain if you want help, and return to the lesson before practice when a topic needs review.

## storyScenes/chapter9-mission1-scene3

A required payment could affect what a household had available for its other needs. Goods required materials and work. Money required access to money. To explain the burden, we need more than the size of a demand: we also need to know what resources people had and what conditions they faced. This mission does not assign one experience to every family.

Try a fictional comparison, not a historical tax rate. Household A has ten supply tokens and Household B has five. Both must give two. A has eight left and B has three. The same number taken leaves different amounts available.

The tokens stand for resources only; they are not pesos, real tribute rates or points earned for taking goods. To explain an actual case, find evidence about the demand and the household circumstances.

Open the three clues. Then choose the explanation they support. Use Explain if you want help, and return to the lesson before practice when a topic needs review.

## storyScenes/chapter9-mission1-scene4

A rule can describe what an authority demanded. A collection record can describe what was received. These are related questions, but they are not the same. A rule alone does not prove that every demanded payment was collected. A recorded collection alone does not settle whether it followed the rule or how it affected the people who paid.

Our fictional source desk has three cards: a payment instruction, a collection entry, and a complaint about an extra demand. The instruction helps identify the rule. The entry helps identify a recorded action.

The complaint helps identify a reported problem; it does not by itself show how the problem was finally resolved. Compare the cards rather than treating any one as a complete account. Colonial writers had their own purposes, and their records may leave local voices out.

Open the three clues. Then choose the explanation they support. Use Explain if you want help, and return to the lesson before practice when a topic needs review.

## storyScenes/chapter9-mission1-scene5

Spanish colonial rule lasted for a long period, and taxation did not stay unchanged throughout it. Historian Filomeno Aguilars study identifies the ending of tribute in 1884 and the introduction of cedulas personales in 1885. A cedula personal was connected with a later personal-tax system. Keep these two stages distinct instead of treating every colonial payment as the same rule.

The study explains that the later system used rates connected with economic capacity. That does not mean taxation ended, that every person paid the same amount, or that everyone welcomed the change.

Our timeline marks the transition described in this study; it is not a complete chart of every tax. A real payment record still needs its own date, category and setting. We are comparing historical systems, not giving instructions about modern taxes.

Open the three clues. Then choose the explanation they support. Use Explain if you want help, and return to the lesson before practice when a topic needs review.

## storyScenes/chapter9-mission1-scene6

Review five ideas from this mission. Tribute was a required colonial payment rather than simply a gift. Payments could include goods in particular settings. The burden depended on available resources as well as the demand. Rules and recorded collections answer different questions. Tax systems also changed over time.

Prepare a fictional museum report for another Grade 5 learner. State what was demanded, identify the supporting source and explain what you cannot yet know. If you use the two-token household model, label it as a model. It is not a historical tribute rate. Do not assume all households had the same experience or that payment proves agreement.

The mission quiz has 5 questions. Answer at least 3 correctly to pass and earn the mission reward once. If you need help, revisit the linked lesson, practise and retry. Complete all 5 chapter missions, then pass the chapter challenge to finish the chapter.

## storyScenes/chapter9-mission2-scene1

Polo y servicios was a system of required labor during Spanish colonial rule. An authority could call on people to carry out work. Required service is different from choosing to volunteer. To explain a case, ask who ordered the work, who had to do it, where it took place and which rules applied then. Rules, exemptions and actual practice should not be treated as identical throughout the whole colonial period.

A fictional source card orders workers to report for a project. It tells us about a demand for labor. It does not prove that every worker agreed or that every person named actually arrived. We are studying how authority affected people.

This is not a classroom work order: students will not assign forced work to classmates or earn rewards for doing so. Read the instruction, then ask what evidence would show the work actually carried out.

Open the three clues and choose the explanation they support. Use Explain for help. If this topic needs review, revisit its lesson before targeted practice.

## storyScenes/chapter9-mission2-scene2

Required labor could take time away from household work and other needs. Travel could add to the time spent on a task. The effect depended on the work, distance, season and support available at home. We should investigate those conditions rather than assume that every household experienced the same burden. A project could serve colonial aims while placing demands on the people who worked on it.

Try a fictional schedule model. A household has six task slots. If two are assigned to travel and required work, four remain for other tasks. The slots are not historical days or a universal legal requirement.

They show that time used in one place is unavailable for another task at the same moment. Compare the model with evidence about an actual case before describing what families lost or how they responded. Do not ask classmates to disclose private family problems.

Open the three clues and choose the explanation they support. Use Explain for help. If this topic needs review, revisit its lesson before targeted practice.

## storyScenes/chapter9-mission2-scene3

Bandala concerned agricultural products that people were required to supply to the colonial government. It is often described as a forced sale. The word sale must not make us assume the producer freely chose the transaction. A requirement to deliver produce is different from a requirement to provide labor, even though one household could face more than one kind of demand.

Imagine two fictional records. One calls workers to a project. The other orders a delivery of rice. Classify the demand first: labor service or produce delivery. Then ask how it was carried out.

A delivery order does not establish that every producer delivered, that a promised price was paid, or that the transaction was fair. We use a labelled teaching bundle rather than an authentic delivery document or a universal quota.

The details need a particular place and period.

Open the three clues and choose the explanation they support. Use Explain for help. If this topic needs review, revisit its lesson before targeted practice.

## storyScenes/chapter9-mission2-scene4

When investigating compulsory produce delivery, separate the demand, the delivery and the payment. A promise to pay is not the same as payment received. A delivery receipt can show goods were handed over without proving that the producer received the promised money. A complaint may report a problem, but the final outcome needs follow-up evidence.

Our fictional evidence desk contains a rice order, a delivery note and a promise of later payment. Together they support an account of what was demanded and recorded as delivered. They do not establish that the promise was fulfilled.

Ask for an appropriate payment record and compare dates and amounts for the same transaction. Do not invent a price or assume that every bandala transaction ended in the same way. Learning points reward a supported explanation, not taking produce from other people.

Open the three clues and choose the explanation they support. Use Explain for help. If this topic needs review, revisit its lesson before targeted practice.

## storyScenes/chapter9-mission2-scene5

The NHCP registry identifies Agustin Sumuroy with Palapag, Samar, and an uprising beginning on 1 June 1649 against forced labor and abuses. This gives us a named case of opposition to colonial demands. It does not mean every worker everywhere responded in the same way. Keep a leader, location, period and stated issue connected in your explanation.

The NCCA CulturEd account connects the workers problem with being compelled to go to Cavite for shipbuilding. Distance matters here: a demand could involve leaving the home area.

We do not need to invent speeches or act out fighting to understand why the demand mattered. Our source guide is a modern learning aid, not a diary written by a worker.

Explain the connection between labor, distance and protest, and identify what these short accounts do not tell us about each persons experience.

Open the three clues and choose the explanation they support. Use Explain for help. If this topic needs review, revisit its lesson before targeted practice.

## storyScenes/chapter9-mission2-scene6

Review the five ideas from this mission. Polo concerned required labor service. Time and travel could affect other household tasks. Bandala concerned compulsory produce delivery. A demand, a delivery and a payment promise are different stages. Sumuroys case shows a named response to forced labor and abuses.

Imagine a fictional museum desk with a work order, a rice-delivery note and a payment promise. Classify each one, explain what it supports and say what still needs checking. Do not call forced work volunteering or treat a promise as money already received. The six-slot schedule is a model, not a legal quota. Keep actual claims tied to their place and period.

## storyScenes/chapter9-mission3-scene1

Agriculture supplied food, materials and products for sale. A household could use part of a harvest at home and exchange another part. A crop grown for sale is often called a cash crop.

The name describes its purpose in a transaction, not a promise that the grower became wealthy. Food crops could also be sold. We should ask how a harvest was used instead of dividing all plants into two fixed groups.

Imagine a fictional harvest card showing rice kept for meals and rice offered for sale. The same crop serves different needs.

Selling part of it may bring money, but a sales total alone does not tell us what the household spent on seed, tools or transport. Nor does it show the food left at home.

This model is a teaching example, not a surviving farm account. Look for the use, the work and the resources involved before explaining a household economy.

Open the three evidence clues, then choose the explanation they support. Use Explain if you want help. Review this lesson before targeted practice when the topic needs another look.

## storyScenes/chapter9-mission3-scene2

An economic policy can affect what people produce, who they may sell to and what resources an authority receives. A policy has an aim, but its aim is not proof of its actual results. To investigate one, connect the rule with records of what people did and how it affected them. Different groups might gain or lose in different ways.

Try a fictional market comparison. In Card A, growers can choose among several buyers. In Card B, a rule requires delivery to one authorized buyer. Even without inventing a price, you can see a difference in choice.

The cards are models, not descriptions of all markets during Spanish rule. For an actual policy, ask which product, place and period it covered. A rule about one crop does not establish control over every product everywhere.

Open the three evidence clues, then choose the explanation they support. Use Explain if you want help. Review this lesson before targeted practice when the topic needs another look.

## storyScenes/chapter9-mission3-scene3

The tobacco monopoly is a named example of colonial economic control. The NHCP historical marker dates its formal establishment to March 1782 under Governor Jose Basco y Vargas. It also records abolition in 1882. These dates identify this policy period; they do not mean tobacco farming itself began and ended on those dates.

Wolters describes compulsory cultivation in designated districts and government purchase of the crop at an officially determined price. This restricted growers choices about production and sale. Do not turn designated districts into a claim about every farm in all the islands.

Our diagram shows a simplified relationship between growers and the government, not a map of every covered district. We study the crop to understand colonial power. This lesson does not encourage growing, handling or using tobacco.

Open the three evidence clues, then choose the explanation they support. Use Explain if you want help. Review this lesson before targeted practice when the topic needs another look.

## storyScenes/chapter9-mission3-scene4

A policy could bring revenue to the government while placing burdens on growers. Revenue means income received; it is not the same as profit after expenses. To explain effects on a household, ask about work, materials, the price received and available choices. A large government collection alone cannot prove that all growers benefited.

Use a fictional account model with no historical price claim. A grower receives eight tokens from a sale and has five tokens of costs. Three remain after those listed costs. Another card showing only eight received leaves the costs unknown.

The tokens are not pesos, crop quotas or points earned by controlling other people. In an actual case, look for dated accounts and consider whether some costs or unpaid work are missing. A simple total cannot tell us every experience.

Open the three evidence clues, then choose the explanation they support. Use Explain if you want help. Review this lesson before targeted practice when the topic needs another look.

## storyScenes/chapter9-mission3-scene5

Policies could change or end. Abolition of the tobacco monopoly ended that particular government arrangement; it did not mean that all farming, trade or taxation stopped. A date tells us when an institutional change is recorded. To explain what followed, we need evidence about later activity as well as the earlier rule.

Imagine a fictional exhibit with three cards: an old monopoly instruction, a later abolition notice and a farm account after the change. The instruction helps explain a required arrangement. The notice records an institutional ending. The farm account helps investigate later production and exchange.

Do not ask one card to answer every question. Keep an official aim separate from implementation, and compare how particular people experienced the transition instead of assuming everyone gained equally.

Open the three evidence clues, then choose the explanation they support. Use Explain if you want help. Review this lesson before targeted practice when the topic needs another look.

## storyScenes/chapter9-mission3-scene6

Review five ideas. Harvests could serve household and market needs. Economic rules could affect choices about production and buyers. The tobacco monopoly is a named, dated example of government control. Revenue and income remaining after costs are different questions. A policy ending does not mean all economic activity ended.

Prepare a fictional museum report for another Grade 5 learner. Name a policy, identify a supporting clue and explain its scope. Compare a government aim with evidence about growers experiences. If you use the eight-minus-five token model, label it as a teaching model rather than a historical crop price. Do not present every community as identical or treat every recorded receipt as profit.

The mission quiz has 5 questions. Answer at least 3 correctly to pass and earn the mission reward once. If you need help, revisit the linked lesson, practise and retry. Complete all 5 chapter missions, then pass the chapter challenge to finish the chapter.

## storyScenes/chapter9-mission4-scene1

The Manila-Acapulco galleon trade connected the Philippines and Mexico across the Pacific Ocean. Acapulco was a port in New Spain, in what is now Mexico. The trade is commonly dated 1565-1815. These dates describe this trading connection, not the beginning or end of all Philippine trade. Earlier lessons already showed people exchanging goods before Spanish rule.

Our route diagram connects named places with arrows. It is a relationship guide, not a navigation chart: real voyages did not follow a straight line across a small page. Wind, currents and the direction of travel mattered.

Trace Manila to Acapulco, then trace the connection back. A line can show a link between ports without telling us the time, cargo or outcome of every crossing. To investigate a particular voyage, look for its own dated records.

## storyScenes/chapter9-mission4-scene2

Asian goods such as silk and porcelain traveled through Manila toward Acapulco. Silver moved from the Americas toward Manila, helping pay for goods. Manila was a meeting point within a wider network: goods leaving its port were not necessarily all made in the Philippines. Ask where an item was produced as well as which port shipped it.

Try a fictional cargo-card sort. A card says porcelain was loaded in Manila, but does not name its maker. Another card identifies an item as made in China. The loading port and production place answer different questions.

Our symbols stand for examples, not the complete contents of a particular ship. A cargo list also cannot prove that every item arrived, that every voyage carried the same mixture, or that all people shared the proceeds.

Compare departure and arrival records when the question concerns delivery.

## storyScenes/chapter9-mission4-scene3

A ship and its cargo depended on people. Makers produced goods, workers prepared supplies, crews handled voyages, and traders arranged exchange. Obispados study of the sixteenth-century trade discusses household production, weaving and work related to moving cargo. Seeing a valuable object should lead us to ask about the work behind it, not only its selling price.

Our fictional task cards identify making cloth, preparing a ship and recording cargo. These are different roles in a connected system. One person could perform more than one role, and the work should not be described as identical for every place and period.

An account naming a merchant may leave other workers unnamed. Do not conclude that unnamed people did no work. Earlier lessons also showed that colonial labor demands could be compulsory; a cargo value alone tells us neither consent nor fair payment.

## storyScenes/chapter9-mission4-scene4

A long sea crossing involved uncertainty. Weather, ship condition, supplies and other dangers could affect a voyage. A departure entry records a ship leaving; it does not guarantee arrival or show the whole journey. The National Archives account of the Nuestra Senora de Covadonga illustrates how a particular ships papers can open questions about cargo and a voyage affected by capture.

We do not reenact an attack or award points for harm. Instead, use a fictional source desk: a departure note, a cargo list and a later arrival entry. Check that they concern the same vessel and journey before connecting them.

A successful arrival does not prove that every crossing was safe; a loss does not prove every voyage failed. The teaching ship is a symbol, not a reconstruction of that named vessel. Your task is to explain what each record supports and what remains unknown.

Open the three clues and choose the explanation they support. Use Explain for help, or revisit the lesson before targeted practice if a topic needs review.

## storyScenes/chapter9-mission4-scene5

The trading connection moved objects, money and ideas across places. The Metropolitan Museum discusses how Asian goods could influence art in the Americas. A connection can change what people make and use. But the presence of valuable cargo is not proof that every person or community became wealthy. Benefits, costs and choices need evidence about the people involved.

Imagine a fictional comparison desk. A merchant card records receipts, while a worker card lists time spent and payment owed. The first does not answer the second.

To compare effects, ask what each person received, what costs they faced and how much choice they had. A modern collection object may help investigate design and exchange, but it is not a complete household budget.

Nor did the end of the galleon connection in 1815 mean all Philippine trade stopped. Keep the network and its limits visible together.

Open the three clues and choose the explanation they support. Use Explain for help, or revisit the lesson before targeted practice if a topic needs review.

## storyScenes/chapter9-mission4-scene6

Review five ideas. Manila and Acapulco were linked across the Pacific. Goods and silver moved through a wider network. Production places and loading ports were not always the same. People worked to make and move cargo. Departure and arrival were different stages, and valuable trade did not prove equal benefits for everyone.

Prepare a fictional exhibit report for another Grade 5 learner. Name the connection, identify a supporting clue and explain a limit. If you use the route diagram, call it a schematic rather than an exact sailing track. Keep workers visible alongside cargo, and compare peoples receipts, costs and choices before describing effects. Do not turn one journey into every voyage or treat 1815 as the end of all Philippine exchange.

## storyScenes/chapter9-mission5-scene1

Colonial economic demands affected resources that households used for food, work and other needs. Tribute, required labor and compulsory produce delivery were different demands. To explain an effect, identify the demand first. Then ask what resources were available and what remained afterward. A payment record alone does not reveal the whole household situation.

Consider a fictional comparison. Household A begins with twelve supply tokens and Household B with seven. Each gives three under the same model demand. Nine remain for A and four for B.

This does not tell us every need or cost, but it shows why equal amounts taken do not automatically mean equal burdens. The tokens are not pesos, rice measures or actual tribute rates.

In a real investigation, use dated evidence about the demand, resources and needs. Do not ask classmates to disclose family finances.

Open the three clues, then choose an explanation they support. Use Explain for help. Revisit the lesson before targeted practice if the topic needs another look.

## storyScenes/chapter9-mission5-scene2

A demand for work could affect household tasks differently depending on when and where it occurred. Travel could increase time away. Work during a busy farming period could leave fewer people or less time for other tasks. This is a connection to investigate, not a claim that every demand produced an identical result. Ask what work was needed, who could do it and what support was available.

Our fictional calendar has eight work slots. Three are assigned to travel and required service, leaving five for the other listed tasks. The slots are not historical service days or a universal legal rule.

Compare the schedule with evidence for a particular place and period before describing actual consequences. The same instruction might meet different household conditions. A finished project does not by itself prove that every worker benefited, consented or had no other responsibilities.

Open the three clues, then choose an explanation they support. Use Explain for help. Revisit the lesson before targeted practice if the topic needs another look.

## storyScenes/chapter9-mission5-scene3

An economic rule could shape what growers produced or where they could sell. Earlier lessons used the tobacco monopoly as a named example. Wolters describes designated districts with compulsory cultivation and official purchase. The important question here is how a rule affected available choices, not whether a grower appeared in a trading account.

Try a fictional comparison desk. Card A allows a producer to choose among several buyers. Card B requires delivery to an authorized buyer. Card B limits the choice of buyer even if it lists a payment. Payment and freedom to choose are different questions.

Neither card alone tells us the full household outcome, price fairness or every local response. Use records of the particular rule and actual transaction. This exercise does not encourage tobacco use or reward students for imposing demands on others.

## storyScenes/chapter9-mission5-scene4

A policy or trade connection could bring income to one group while another faced costs, uncertain payment or reduced choice. Government revenue, a merchants receipts and a workers household resources answer different questions. Do not treat one large total as evidence that every community benefited equally. Ask whose experience a record actually describes.

Obispados study of early galleon trade keeps household production and cargo work visible alongside goods.

Use that reminder when looking at a fictional evidence desk: a merchant ledger records receipts, a makers card describes materials and labor, and a workers note raises a payment question. Compare each record within its own setting.

Missing names are not proof that no one else contributed. The exercise does not establish that every merchant gained or every worker had the same loss; particular claims still need evidence.

## storyScenes/chapter9-mission5-scene5

People could respond to demands in different ways, including raising complaints or organizing opposition. The NHCP marker connects Sumuroy in Palapag, Samar, with an uprising against forced labor and abuses beginning on 1 June 1649. This named example links an economic demand with a response. It does not describe every community or every persons private reason.

For a fictional source task, compare a complaint with a later decision about the same issue. The complaint identifies a reported problem; the decision may help investigate what followed.

A complaint alone does not prove success, and silence in an official account does not prove universal agreement. Explain the recorded action and say what remains unknown. We do not reenact fighting or award points for harm.

Your report should make peoples actions visible without inventing speeches or claiming a single response for all communities.

Open the three clues, then choose an explanation they support. Use Explain for help. Revisit the lesson before targeted practice if the topic needs another look.

## storyScenes/chapter9-mission5-scene6

Connect the chapters five missions. Tribute concerned required payments; polo concerned labor service; bandala concerned compulsory produce delivery. Agricultural rules could restrict production and buyers. The galleon network linked goods and peoples work across places. To explain effects, ask what happened to resources, time and choices, and whose experience the evidence describes.

Prepare a fictional museum report for another Grade 5 learner. Name a demand, identify the people and setting, give a supporting clue and state a limit. Compare household needs and resources instead of treating one total as every persons experience. Label token and calendar models as models. Check a complaint separately from its outcome, and do not invent private motives.

## storyScenes/mission2-scene1

In the previous mission, you investigated how people organized community life. Now follow a new problem: how can families obtain food and useful goods when no one can make everything alone? We will connect resources, skills, products and exchange.

A livelihood is work that helps people meet their needs. Farming, fishing and craft work could contribute in different ways. Suitable land or nearby water offers opportunities, but people also need knowledge, tools and cooperation. Not everyone in one place has the same job.

Worked example: a family has suitable soil and water. Step 1. Prepare the growing area and plant crops. Step 2. Care for the plants using farming knowledge. Step 3. Gather the harvest and plan how much the family needs.

This connects a resource with work and a product: land and water, farming skills, then food. Crops and methods differed among communities; the example is not a record of one named historical village.

## storyScenes/prologue-mission3-scene4

Time information answers different questions. A research timeline tells us when modern study happened: National Museum investigations at Tabon included 1962 to 1965; the Homo luzonensis description was published in 2019. These dates do not mean the ancient people lived then.

An age estimate describes how old a find may be. A range gives limits rather than one exact year. With years ago, a larger number means farther into the past.

Try the clearly fictional range exercise. Find A is estimated at 1,000 to 2,000 years ago. Find B is estimated at 1,500 to 2,500 years ago. The ranges overlap from 1,500 to 2,000.

You cannot be certain which find is older using these ranges alone. These are made-up numbers for practice, not dates for Tabon or Callao. The oldest evidence found so far is not necessarily the first person who arrived.
